title: The next phase of quantum energy science: from mechanisms to applications
authors: Florian Metzler, Matt K. Lilley, Matthew C. DeCapua, Peter L. Hagelstein, Jonah F. Messinger, Nicola Galvanetto
abstract: A growing research community spanning quantum batteries, molecular and excitonic energy transport, polaritonics, quantum materials and nuclear control has begun to describe its work in terms of quantum energy or quantum energy science. What connects these otherwise disparate efforts is the deliberate use of quantum states, couplings, collective effects and engineered environments to control energetic states and pathways. A key difference from quantum information science is that the complete quantum state does not always need to be preserved; engineered dissipation or dephasing can even improve the desired outcome. We organize this emerging domain through a framework that connects mechanisms, functions, capabilities, and applications. We identify five elementary functions (Excite, Hold, Release, Transfer, and Transform) and examine the mechanisms that implement them. The same functions recur from the molecular to the nuclear scale, although their relative implementation difficulty can differ sharply. Moving toward technology, we highlight three engineering capabilities (Storage, Routing, and Conversion) through the performance metrics that matter for their applications. Stretch scenarios illustrate what performance targets could make these capabilities technologically consequential.
summary: This paper establishes a unifying framework for 'quantum energy science,' which focuses on controlling energy flow rather than just preserving quantum states. It categorizes this field using five core functions—Excite, Hold, Release, Transfer, and Transform—that apply across vastly different physical systems, from molecules to the atomic nucleus. This framework is crucial for guiding future research toward practical energy technologies.
main_problem: The paper aims to develop a comprehensive framework for 'quantum energy science' to control energetic states and pathways, distinguishing this field from quantum information science.
main_result: It organizes the field around five elementary functions (Excite, Hold, Release, Transfer, Transform) and three engineering capabilities (Storage, Routing, Conversion), providing a shared vocabulary for the community.
method: The authors develop a conceptual framework connecting mechanisms to functions, capabilities, and applications, drawing analogies across energy scales from molecular to nuclear.
model_or_system: The framework applies to diverse systems, including quantum batteries, molecular excitons, polaritons, and nuclear energy transitions (e.g., involving isotopes like ${}^{229}	ext{Th}$).
key_observables: Energy recovered, power, storage time, decay rates, and coupling strengths are key performance metrics.
important_parameters: Energy scales range from eV (molecular) to keV–MeV (nuclear); time scales span from fast dynamics to years (nuclear isomers).
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that controlling energy flow via quantum mechanisms (like engineered dissipation) can be systematically categorized and improved upon.
figures_summary: Figure 1 maps the relationship from mechanisms to applications, while Figure 2 illustrates the five elementary energetic functions.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the concept, defines the five elementary functions (Excite, Hold, Release, Transfer, Transform), details the mechanisms implementing them, and concludes by highlighting the engineering capabilities (Storage, Routing, Conversion) and future technological targets.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it provides a unifying conceptual structure for diverse areas of open quantum systems, connecting concepts from quantum optics, energy harvesting, and nuclear physics under a single functional paradigm.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Maps out key relationships from mechanisms to applications in quantum energy science. Forward arrows link mechanisms, functions, capabilities/performance metrics and applications; lower arrows show how performance and application requirements guide design. The applications shown are the illustrative stretch scenarios in Table 3.

Figure 2. Five elementary energetic functions. The central sketches are illustrative: ﬁlled dots mark initial occupation, and |𝑔⟩and |𝑒⟩denote ground and excited states. On the right, 𝐴and 𝐵denote subsystems and an asterisk marks excitation. 𝐸in and 𝐸out indicate energy entering and leaving the system. 𝐶denotes a different energetic carrier or physical conﬁguration, illustrated here by charge separation.

Figure 3. Implementation difﬁculty across transition-energy regimes. Energy ranges are schematic. Colors indicate qualitative difﬁculty for representative systems. The lower arrows indicate broad trends toward more demanding direct control and greater potential energetic leverage at higher transition energies.
Figure 3 suggests a design strategy: exploit the functions that a platform provides naturally and engineer the missing ones.
